label: Fire at will
desc: Controlled fire: cooking, warmth, light, clearing land and later every kiln and furnace. The first energy technology.

label: Firewood
desc: Wood burned as fuel, the main source of heat until coal; one to two tonnes a person a year in organic economies (part 01).

label: Charcoal
desc: Wood charred in clamps by colliers; a hotter, lighter fuel for smelting and smithing. A bloomery took 10 to 18 kg of charcoal for each kg of iron (part 03, from memory), so metal was bound to woodland until coke. Wood charred in clamps; a hotter, lighter fuel for smelting and smithing. Bound metal to woodland until coke.

label: Draught animals
desc: Oxen, then horses, pulling ploughs, carts and mills; the largest non-human power source before water and wind.

label: Watermill
desc: About 6,000 in England's Domesday survey of 1086 and about 10,000 by 1300 (part 01). A wheel turned by a stream, driving grinding, fulling, bellows, hammers and saws; shared streams made it a chokepoint.

label: Windmill
desc: Wind-driven mill for grinding and drainage, spreading where streams were scarce.

label: Peat
desc: Dug bog fuel; powered the Dutch Golden Age's industries before coal.

label: Coal
desc: Mineral fuel, used in Han and Song China and dug in England from the 13th century. About half of England's energy by 1700 and over 90% by 1850 (part 01), ending the organic economy's land limit. Mineral fuel; half of England's energy by about 1700 and over 90% by 1850, ending the organic economy's land limit.

label: Coke
desc: Coal baked to drive off impurities; replaced charcoal in the blast furnace (Darby, 1709) and freed iron from the woods.

label: Steam engine
desc: Heat into motion: Newcomen pumping, Watt's separate condenser, then high-pressure engines for mills, rail and ships.

label: Oil
desc: Crude petroleum, first refined for kerosene lamps; later fuel, lubricants, asphalt and petrochemicals.

label: Natural gas
desc: Methane from wells, piped for heat, power and as feedstock for ammonia.

label: Electricity
desc: Power carried by wire: lighting, motors, electrochemistry; separated where power is made from where it is used.

label: Electric grid
desc: Interconnected generation and transmission; central stations, alternating current, and later national grids.

label: Internal combustion engine
desc: Fuel burned inside the cylinder (Otto, Diesel); compact power for vehicles, tractors and aircraft.

label: Nuclear power
desc: Fission heat raising steam for electricity.

label: Solar and wind power
desc: Photovoltaic and wind-turbine generation, cheap at scale from the 2010s.

label: Foraging
desc: Gathering wild plants and small game; the economy of more than 99% of human history.

label: Hunting
desc: Taking wild animals with spears, then bows, traps and drives; high-skill, shared returns.

label: Fishing
desc: Taking fish and shellfish with hooks, nets, traps and weirs.

label: Cereal farming
desc: Domesticated wheat, barley, rice and maize; storable grain that fed more people per hectare than foraging.

label: Herding domesticates
desc: Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs kept for meat, then milk, wool and traction.

label: Dairying
desc: Milk, butter and cheese: the secondary products of herds.

label: Wool sheep
desc: Sheep bred for fleece; wool became the raw material of the largest pre-industrial industry.

label: Plough
desc: Ard, then the heavy mouldboard plough; turned draught power into tilled land.

label: Irrigation farming
desc: Fields watered by canals and basins; high yields bound to collective water works.

label: Three-field rotation
desc: Winter grain, spring grain and fallow in rotation on open fields.

label: Legumes and clover
desc: Nitrogen-fixing crops in rotation that raised grain yields and fed more beasts.

label: Manure
desc: Dung returned to fields: the main nitrogen source until guano and synthetic fertiliser.

label: Flour milling
desc: Grinding grain: quern, then mill; the lord's mill and its toll.

label: Baking
desc: Bread ovens; in towns a licensed trade, on manors often the lord's oven.

label: Brewing
desc: Ale and beer from malted grain; barley's sink and a household then commercial industry.

label: Salting and curing
desc: Salt used to keep meat and fish; tied food stores to the salt trade.

label: Cold chain
desc: Mechanical refrigeration, refrigerated rail cars and ships carrying meat and produce across oceans.

label: Synthetic nitrogen
desc: Haber–Bosch ammonia; fertiliser now feeding 40 to 50% of people and separating herds from fields.

label: Tractor
desc: Engine-powered traction replacing horses and the land that fed them.

label: Meatpacking
desc: Disassembly lines and refrigerated distribution from stockyard cities; later highly concentrated.

label: Supermarket
desc: Self-service retail with central buying and its own supply chains.

label: Green Revolution
desc: High-yield varieties with fertiliser and irrigation, raising grain yields across Asia and Latin America.

label: Stone tools
desc: Flaked flint and stone for cutting, scraping and points; the oldest manufactured goods.

label: Pottery
desc: Fired clay vessels for storage and cooking.

label: Kiln
desc: A controlled high-temperature firing chamber for pottery, lime and later metal.

label: Lime
desc: Burnt limestone for mortar, plaster, tanning and soil.

label: Glass
desc: A forest glassworks burned 150 to 200 kg of wood for each kg of glass (part 01). Sand, soda or potash and lime fused with heavy fuel use.

label: Rendering and tallow
desc: Animal fat rendered into tallow for candles, soap and grease.

label: Alkali (soda)
desc: Soda and potash from plant ash and kelp, later Leblanc and Solvay processes; for glass, soap and bleaching.

label: Sulphuric acid
desc: The base chemical of the chemical industry: bleaching, soda, fertiliser.

label: Coal-tar chemicals
desc: By-products of gasworks and coke ovens turned into dyes, drugs and later plastics.

label: Plastics
desc: Synthetic polymers from coal tar, then petroleum feedstocks.

label: Cement and concrete
desc: Portland cement and concrete, later reinforced with steel.

label: Timber
desc: Wood for building, ships and tools.

label: Coppice
desc: Woodland cut on rotation for poles, withies and charcoal wood.

label: Rubber
desc: Vulcanised natural rubber for belts, hoses and tyres.

label: Paper
desc: Pulped fibre sheets, from China; carrier of records, print and paper money.

label: Salt making
desc: Salt from brine boiling, evaporation pans or mines; a fuel-hungry trade.

label: Copper smelting
desc: Reducing copper ore with charcoal; the first metallurgy.

label: Tin
desc: Rare ore, alloyed with copper for bronze; traded across long distances.

label: Bronze
desc: Copper–tin alloy; tools, weapons and status goods dependent on tin routes.

label: Bloomery iron
desc: Iron reduced in a small furnace with charcoal and hammered.

label: Blast furnace
desc: Tall water-blown furnace making liquid cast iron.

label: Puddling
desc: Cort's process turning pig iron into wrought iron with coal.

label: Bessemer steel
desc: Air blown through molten iron made cheap bulk steel.

label: Open-hearth steel
desc: Siemens–Martin regenerative furnace steel.

label: Electric arc steel
desc: Steel melted from scrap with electric arcs.

label: Aluminium
desc: Hall–Héroult electrolysis made aluminium cheap with large electricity inputs.

label: Machine tools
desc: Lathes, borers and planers making precise metal parts.

label: Interchangeable parts
desc: Parts made to gauge so any one fits; the basis of mass production.

label: Spinning
desc: Twisting fibre into thread, by spindle, then wheel.

label: Weaving
desc: Interlacing thread into cloth on a loom.

label: Cotton
desc: Cotton fibre, from India; later the core of the industrial revolution and of slave plantations.

label: Flax and linen
desc: Flax retted and spun into linen.

label: Fulling mill
desc: Water-driven hammers to finish woollen cloth.

label: Mechanised spinning
desc: Jenny, water frame and mule.

label: Power loom
desc: Mechanised weaving.

label: Dyeing
desc: Colouring cloth with plant, insect and later synthetic dyes and mordants.

label: Synthetic fibres
desc: Nylon and polyester from petrochemicals.

label: Tanning
desc: Hides into leather with bark tannin, later chrome salts.

label: Wattle and daub
desc: Woven withies plastered with clay and dung.

label: Mudbrick
desc: Sun-dried clay bricks.

label: Stone masonry
desc: Cut stone building.

label: Fired brick
desc: Kiln-fired clay bricks.

label: Steel frame
desc: Skyscraper construction on a steel skeleton.

label: Passenger lift
desc: Safety lifts that made tall buildings usable.

label: Piped water
desc: Mains water supply to houses.

label: Sewers
desc: Underground sewerage removing waste from cities.

label: Boats
desc: Rafts, dugouts and hide boats.

label: Sail
desc: Wind-driven ships.

label: Pack animals
desc: Donkeys, camels and horses carrying loads.

label: Wheel and cart
desc: Wheeled vehicles drawn by animals.

label: Roads
desc: Built routes for carts and armies.

label: Canals
desc: Artificial waterways.

label: Railway
desc: Steam locomotives on iron rails.

label: Steamship
desc: Steam-propelled ships.

label: Motor vehicle
desc: Cars and lorries with internal combustion engines.

label: Container shipping
desc: Standard boxes moved between ship, rail and truck.

label: Aviation
desc: Powered flight, then airlines and air freight.

label: Pipelines
desc: Pipes moving oil, gas and water.

label: Gift exchange
desc: Goods moved by gift and obligation.

label: Redistribution
desc: A centre collecting goods and handing them out.

label: Barter
desc: Direct exchange of goods for goods.

label: Credit and accounts
desc: Debts recorded in units of account.

label: Coinage
desc: Stamped metal coins.

label: Markets and fairs
desc: Regular places and days for trade.

label: Bills of exchange
desc: Transferable orders to pay at a distance.

label: Banking
desc: Deposit and lending houses.

label: Paper money
desc: Notes as money.

label: Joint-stock company
desc: Shares in a permanent company.

label: Stock exchange
desc: A market for shares.

label: Insurance
desc: Pooled risk for a premium.

label: Central bank
desc: A state's bank.

label: Electronic payments
desc: Card and digital payment networks.

label: Long-distance trade
desc: Goods moved far beyond home.

label: Household production
desc: The household as the unit of production and consumption.

label: Property in land
desc: Rights to land held and transferred.

label: Lordship and the manor
desc: Lords' rights over land and tenants.

label: Serfdom
desc: Tenants bound to land and labour dues.

label: Slavery
desc: People owned as property.

label: Guilds
desc: Associations of craftsmen or merchants.

label: Wage labour
desc: Work sold for wages.

label: Putting-out
desc: Merchants supplying materials to home workers.

label: Factory system
desc: Workers gathered at powered machines under supervision.

label: State taxation
desc: A state taking a share of output.

label: Law courts
desc: Third-party enforcement of rights and debts.

label: Trade unions
desc: Workers organised to bargain.

label: Corporation
desc: Limited-liability companies with managers.

label: Welfare state
desc: State insurance, pensions and services.

label: Cities
desc: Dense settlements living on supply from elsewhere.

label: Writing
desc: Marks on clay and papyrus.

label: Record keeping
desc: Tokens and tallies.

label: Printing
desc: Woodblock printing in Tang China, movable type in Song China and Korea, and in Europe from about 1450; it carried paper money, prices, contracts and manuals.

label: Postal service
desc: Regular carriage of letters.

label: Telegraph
desc: Messages by wire.

label: Telephone
desc: Voice by wire.

label: Radio
desc: Wireless signals.

label: Computer
desc: Programmable electronic calculation.

label: Semiconductors
desc: Transistors and chips.

label: Internet
desc: Packet-switched networks.

label: Mobile phone
desc: Cellular telephones.
